title: The One Everybody Already Built
gist: The default architecture — the one you get by just starting to code. Cheap, simple, familiar, and degrading in every dimension as it grows. Worth knowing precisely, because you will inherit one.
minute: Four standard layers — **presentation, business, persistence, database**. Technically partitioned, so every domain is smeared across all of them. Domain-driven design fits it badly.
**Layers of isolation**: a change in one layer doesn't touch the others, *provided the layers in the request path are closed*. Open a layer and you trade isolation for a shortcut.
The **Architecture Sinkhole** antipattern: requests passing through layers that do nothing. 20% is fine. 80% means the style is wrong for the problem.
Its strengths are **cost and simplicity**; its weaknesses are **deployability, testability, elasticity and scalability**. Every rating starts good and degrades as the codebase grows.
Good for small applications, tight budgets, and as a starting point while you work out whether you need something more complex. **Keep reuse minimal and inheritance shallow** so you can leave later.

sections.alt: Five stacked layers with a services layer marked open and a bypass arrow around it
sections.cap: Fig. 10-1 · a closed layer must be passed through. An open layer may be skipped.
sections.p: Also called n-tiered. It is the de facto standard for legacy applications, and it is what *Architecture by Implication* and *Accidental Architecture* both produce: when a team just starts coding without deciding on a style, this is the style they get.
items: Each layer forms an abstraction around one kind of work. Presentation doesn't know how customer data is fetched; business doesn't know how it will be displayed.

That separation makes role and responsibility models easy, and lets developers work to their technical specialism. **The trade-off is holistic agility** — the system's ability to respond to change as a whole.
Because partitioning is technical, the domain of *customer* lives in presentation, business, rules, services and database at once. Changing that domain means touching every layer.

sections.alt: Three physical topology variants: one unit plus database, UI split off, and everything in one unit
sections.cap: Fig. 10-2 · the logical layers stay the same; only the deployment boundary moves.
sections.p: The third variant — all four layers in one unit with an embedded or in-memory database — is how a great many on-premises products ship to customers, and how mobile applications are built.

sections.t: Presentation wants to read the database directly
sections.alt: Five stacked layers with a services layer marked open and a bypass arrow around it
sections.sit: A screen needs a simple customer lookup. Going presentation → business → persistence → database is slower and more code than reading it directly. In the early 2000s this shortcut had a name: the **Fast-Lane Reader** pattern.
opts: Open the layers so simple reads can skip.

Faster, and it dissolves layers of isolation. Now a change to persistence reaches both business *and* presentation, and you have a tightly coupled, brittle architecture that is difficult and expensive to change.
Keep the layers on the request path closed.
You pay for a hop you didn't need. In exchange, any layer can be replaced without touching the others — swapping the UI framework stays inside presentation, provided contracts hold.
Open one specific layer, deliberately, and document why.
The right move when there's a reason. Adding a **Services layer** for shared business objects only works if that layer is open — otherwise business is forced to route through it to reach persistence.
sections.verdict: The rule is **layers of isolation**: layers involved in the major request flow must be closed, or the isolation is fictional. Which layers are open, which are closed, and *why*, has to be documented — failing to communicate it is how these architectures become brittle, untestable and undeployable.

sections.t: Most requests pass through doing nothing
sections.alt: A request traversing four layers with no logic applied at any of them
sections.sit: You audit the request log. A large share of requests enter presentation, get handed to business unchanged, handed to persistence unchanged, become one SQL call, and return up the stack with nothing added — no aggregation, no calculation, no rules.
opts: Nothing. It's only some of the requests.
Correct, if it really is only some. Every layered architecture has sinkhole scenarios; the 80-20 rule is the usual guide, and around 20% is acceptable.
Open all the layers so simple requests short-circuit.
Fixes the wasted object instantiation and memory. The trade-off you just accepted is that change is now much harder to manage.
Treat it as evidence the style is wrong here.
If 80% of requests are sinkholes, the architecture is doing almost no work per request and charging you for four layers of ceremony to do it.
sections.verdict: The **Architecture Sinkhole antipattern** is not a bug to fix but a ratio to measure. The useful discipline is that you *count* it rather than argue about it — and the count is a genuine signal about whether the style fits the problem domain.

sections.alt: Three physical topology variants: one unit plus database, UI split off, and everything in one unit
sections.cap: One deployment unit means one failure domain and one restart.
items: **Fault tolerance is poor.** One out-of-memory condition anywhere crashes the whole unit. Availability suffers too, because monolithic **mean time to recover** is high — two minutes for a small application, fifteen or more for a large one.

**Governance is unusually good.** The original structural testing tools were built with this style in mind: ArchUnit's `layeredArchitecture()` states exactly which layer may be accessed by which, and enforces open and closed layers on every build.

**Team topologies: it fits all four.** Stream-aligned teams own a flow through every layer. Enabling teams can experiment inside one layer — a new UI library touches only presentation. Complicated-subsystem teams get a clean hook at the persistence layer for analytics.

**The platform team carries the long-term cost.** Keep adding features and, however well partitioned, the monolith eventually strains against database connections, memory, concurrent users or something else — and keeping it running gets progressively harder.

sections.alt: Architecture characteristics ratings for the layered style
sections.cap: Cost and simplicity carry it. Everything else starts adequate and degrades with size.
items: **Use it** for small, simple applications and websites; when budget and time are very tight; and as a starting point while you work out whether something more complex is warranted. It is often the cheapest route to **feasibility** — can we deliver this scope, in this time, with these people?
**Don't use it** once the application is large. Maintainability, agility, testability and deployability all degrade with size, and this is the style that degrades first.
**If you use it as a stepping stone**, keep code reuse minimal and inheritance trees shallow. That is what makes moving to another style later possible rather than theoretical.
sections.p: The style also shows up far outside application code, for exactly the same reason — separation of concerns. Operating systems layer hardware, kernel, system-call interface and user space. TCP/IP layers physical, data link, network, transport and application.

source: Fundamentals of Software Architecture: An Engineering Approach, 2nd ed. — Mark Richards & Neal Ford (O'Reilly, 2025). Chapter 10: Layered Architecture Style, pp. 153–164. Ratings are the chapter's own scorecard.
